openingWhy: Quick is a crew that's run the job a hundred times and moves clean. Hurry is skipping the re-test because the workover rig is standing by and the company man is pacing. Quick gets you home early. Hurry gets you an incident review.
leadershipThought: Vague words create confusion. Precision builds trust and leadership. Say what is true, as clearly as possible. Not emotional. Not exaggerated. Not passive aggressive.

specialFocus.title: The New Standard — Workover Rig Sensor Rig-Up
specialFocus.standardLabel: Why Each Head Sits Where It Sits — Say It With the Picture Up
specialFocus.why:
As of yesterday, Canon has a published standard for how a workover rig location gets sensored up — and it belongs in this week's conversation, because every position in this picture is a Breaking Containment decision.


Walk the crew through it left to right. A workover rig exists to break containment — that's the job. Pulling rods, pulling tubing, opening the well: containment is coming apart on purpose, all day. So the heads go where the breaks happen: the wellhead, where the first break lives. The manifold, where every pressured connection runs. And two heads on the gas buster — because the buster is where broken containment gets sent, flashing gas off the returns the entire job, and the tank is long enough that wind carries a release right past a single head. The controller sits upwind at the trailer with the cascade air, the red zone holds at the source, and now there are two named muster points — primary upwind, secondary crosswind — because the wind owns the first one.

This is the whole week's message in one aerial photo: a controlled break is one where you've already decided where the gas would go and who would know first. The full standard and setup checklist live on the hub's SOPs tab — it's headed to the Breakroom, and from today it's how every workover location gets rigged up.
standard: Head 1 — wellhead/BOP: the first break lives here. The head goes in before the first wrench, not after the first smell.
Head 2 — manifold: every connection under pressure runs through it. Second most likely place containment lets go.
Heads 3 & 4 — gas buster, both ends: the buster is where broken containment goes on purpose. Two heads because the tank is long and the wind doesn't care where you put one.
Controller upwind, red zone flagged, two musters named. Primary upwind, secondary crosswind — pointed out to every hand at the pre-job, not discovered during the muster.
Wind shifts? The plan shifts. The layout is only right for the wind on the sock. When it swings, stop, re-read it, and move what has to move.

scenarios.title: Rig-Up, 6:15 AM
scenarios.body:
You roll onto a workover location at daylight. Rig's already spotted, crew wants to turn to, and you're setting heads. The pusher watches you stake the second head at the gas buster and says, “y'all already got one on that tank — two seems like overkill. We're burning daylight.”

Yesterday, that was a conversation about your judgment. Today it's a conversation about the picture. You pull up the SOP on your phone: four heads, labeled, on an aerial photo of exactly this setup — and the reason out loud: the buster takes the returns all job, the tank is thirty feet long, and a single head only protects the end the wind favors. Not your opinion. Canon's published standard, same on every location, every crew, every time. That's what a standard is for — so the right rig-up doesn't depend on who won an argument at 6:15 in the morning. And notice the other thing it buys you: the pusher who pushed back this morning will watch the next Canon crew stake it exactly the same way — and that's the moment it stops being paperwork and becomes who we are.

questions: Pull the SOP up on your phone right now — everybody. Which of the four heads would you have placed differently before seeing it, and why?
Think about your last workover job: where did the heads actually go? What would this layout have changed?
The buster gets two heads and the wellhead gets one. Somebody explain the reasoning back to me like I'm the newest hand on the crew.
Wind swings 180 mid-job — walk me through it: what moves, who calls it, and where does the crew go while it's moving?
What's the next SOP that deserves this treatment — the setup you do from memory that a new hand couldn't rig from anything written down?
specialFocus.nonNegotiable: Four heads, controller upwind, red zone held, two musters named — every workover location, every time. A controlled break is one where you already decided where the gas would go and who would know first.
